teaser.text: The Toronto-Dominion Bank is a Canadian bank that helps households and businesses hold, move, borrow, invest and protect money. Its business looks simple from the outside, but its earnings depend on what customers pay, what funding costs, and what risks appear later.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for The Toronto-Dominion Bank?

paragraphs.text: Capital available for buybacks, credit losses, net interest margin and savings delivery decide the path. The bear case assumes higher losses and weaker margins; the bull requires faster savings and stronger margins. Repurchases must stay within capital limits while the asset cap constrains U.S. balance-sheet growth.

blocks.heading: How much cash does The Toronto-Dominion Bank really make?

paragraphs.text: Bank funding is part of the operating model. TD takes deposits, pays interest, and uses the money to make loans or buy securities that earn more. That is why enterprise value, net debt, EBITDA, and free cash flow can mislead: they treat funding as separate from the business. Investors instead study returns, capital, liquidity, and net interest margin.

The share count also matters. Stock-based compensation and new-share sales increase it, while repurchases reduce it. The model therefore separates gross dilution from buybacks rather than treating repurchases as a change to the dilution assumption.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for The Toronto-Dominion Bank today?

paragraphs.text: At C$162.23, TD’s market value is C$264,943 million. Its trailing P/E, or price-to-earnings ratio, is 17.4x: investors pay C$17.40 for each dollar earned over the last twelve months. The forward P/E is 16.0x, based on expected earnings. A lower forward multiple means analysts expect higher earnings; it does not mean those earnings have arrived.

blocks.heading: How much does The Toronto-Dominion Bank pay per share?

paragraphs.text: Dividends rose from C$3.16 per share in 2021 to C$4.20 in 2025. Diluted weighted-average shares fell 1.8% in 2025, so adjusted EPS could grow faster than adjusted income. Book value per share reached C$68.78 and tangible book value per share reached C$55.72.

blocks.heading: Does The Toronto-Dominion Bank's dividend come from cash the business makes?

paragraphs.text: TD increased common dividends and began buying back shares. In fiscal 2023 and 2024, distributions exceeded earnings available to common shareholders. That shows current profits did not cover those payments; it does not by itself show that TD lacked regulatory capital. The bank could also draw on earlier retained earnings, excess capital or proceeds from selling investments.

blocks.heading: What could change The Toronto-Dominion Bank's dividend?

paragraphs.text: Management targets 16% adjusted ROE—return on equity, or profit against shareholders’ money—and 7–10% adjusted EPS growth by fiscal 2029. It targets a 40–50% dividend payout range.

The base case gains support if FY2026 earnings and ROE targets hold, provisions continue to fall and repurchases proceed within capital limits. It would move toward the bull case if remediation finishes successfully, regulators ease the constraint, NIM expands and cost savings arrive faster during 2027–2029.

blocks.heading: What has The Toronto-Dominion Bank guided for fiscal 2026?

paragraphs.text: Management targets 16% adjusted ROE—return on equity, or profit against shareholders’ money—and 7–10% adjusted EPS growth by fiscal 2029. It targets a 40–50% dividend payout range.

Credit costs ease, but do not return to pandemic-era lows. Management’s FY2026 PCL guidance is 40–50 basis points. Impaired loans fell from C$5,594M to C$5,143M, while quarterly provisions fell to C$917M. The base steps down from 0.48% to 0.40%; the bear peaks at 0.72%; the bull reaches 0.34%. The bear remains credible because write-offs were still above the prior year and household borrowers face mortgage-payment increases.

blocks.heading: Did The Toronto-Dominion Bank keep its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Chun promised approximately C$8 billion in repurchases, and TD announced completion of that program on January 16, 2026. Management kept that capital-return promise. Its harder promise is lasting control repair, which must survive outside scrutiny. TD is therefore partly on shareholders’ side in its ownership exposure and returned capital, but the board must still prove that pay and oversight match the risks left by the AML failures.

blocks.heading: How have The Toronto-Dominion Bank’s revenue and profit trended?

paragraphs.text: Net interest income rose in every quarter from January 2025 through July 2026. Reported profit was less smooth because the Schwab sale and restructuring charges moved through earnings. July’s reported income growth of 38.3% therefore exceeded adjusted growth of about 21%.

blocks.heading: What should you watch in The Toronto-Dominion Bank’s next results?

paragraphs.text: TD’s next results call is scheduled for December 3, 2026. It will provide a full-year check on earnings, expenses and credit losses, while clarifying how much productivity improvement is financing new investment.
